stem: Which type of blood vessel has valves along its length?

options.rationale: Arteries carry blood at high pressure and have no valves along their length.
Valves in veins stop low-pressure blood flowing backwards.
Capillaries have walls one cell thick and no valves.
Arterioles are small arteries with muscular walls but no valves.

explanation: Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure. Their valves stop it flowing backwards, especially in the legs.
hints: Which vessels carry blood at low pressure?

stem: Which blood vessel has a wall only one cell thick?

options.rationale: The aorta has a very thick, elastic wall.
The vena cava is a large vein with a wall many cells thick.
Arteries have thick walls.
A wall one cell thick gives a short distance for diffusion.

explanation: Capillary walls are one cell thick, so substances have only a short distance to diffuse between the blood and the tissues.
hints: Which vessels exchange substances with the tissues?

stem: True or false: the blood in veins is at a lower pressure than the blood in arteries.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. By the time blood has passed through the capillaries, most of its pressure has been lost.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. Arteries receive blood straight from the ventricles at high pressure; veins carry blood at low pressure after it has passed through the capillaries.

explanation: Blood leaves the ventricles at high pressure in the arteries. Pressure falls as blood passes through the arterioles and capillaries, so blood in veins is at low pressure, which is why veins need valves.
hints: Where along the circulation does blood lose pressure?

stem: (Supplement) Why do arteries have thick walls containing elastic tissue?

options.content: To withstand the high pressure of blood from the heart, stretching and recoiling
options.rationale: This also helps keep blood flowing smoothly between beats.

options.content: To allow oxygen to diffuse quickly into the tissues
options.rationale: Thick walls would slow diffusion; exchange happens in capillaries.
Valves stop backflow, and arteries do not have them along their length.

options.content: Because they carry a larger volume of blood each minute than the veins do
options.rationale: The volume flowing through arteries and veins each minute is the same.

explanation: Arteries carry blood at high pressure in surges. Their thick walls withstand the pressure, and the elastic tissue stretches as each surge arrives and recoils afterwards, maintaining the pressure and evening out the flow.
hints: Think about the pressure of blood just after it leaves the heart.

stem: Name the blood vessel that carries blood away from a kidney.

rejected.feedback: The renal artery brings blood to the kidney.
The ureter carries urine, not blood, away from the kidney.
The vena cava receives blood from the renal vein, but the vessel leaving the kidney is the renal vein.

explanation: The renal artery brings blood to each kidney; the filtered blood leaves in the renal vein, which joins the vena cava.
hints: Vessels of the kidney have the word 'renal' in their names.

stem: What is the function of the valves in veins?

options.content: To pump blood back to the heart
options.rationale: Valves do not pump; muscles squeeze the veins.

options.content: To add oxygen to the blood
options.rationale: Oxygen is added in the lungs.
Blood at low pressure could otherwise flow back, especially in the legs.

options.content: To filter bacteria from the blood
options.rationale: White blood cells and lymph nodes deal with bacteria.

explanation: Blood in veins is at low pressure. Valves allow it to flow only towards the heart and close if it starts to flow backwards.
hints: Valves are one-way doors.

stem: Match each blood vessel with the blood it carries.

right.content: Oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body
Deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs
Oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium
Blood from the aorta to a kidney
Blood from the small intestine to the liver

explanation: The aorta carries oxygenated blood to the body; the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the pulmonary vein returns oxygenated blood to the left atrium; the renal artery supplies a kidney. Blood from the intestine to the liver travels in the hepatic portal vein.
hints: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

stem: (Supplement) Which blood vessel carries oxygenated blood to the liver?

options.rationale: This carries nutrient-rich (but not oxygen-rich) blood from the intestine to the liver.
It branches from the aorta, bringing oxygenated blood.
The hepatic vein carries blood away from the liver.
The renal artery supplies the kidneys.

explanation: The liver receives oxygenated blood from the aorta through the hepatic artery, and nutrient-rich blood from the intestine through the hepatic portal vein. Blood leaves in the hepatic vein.
hints: Oxygenated blood comes from an artery.

stem: (Supplement) How is the structure of a capillary related to its function?

options.content: Its thick muscular wall pumps blood into the tissues.
options.rationale: Capillaries have no muscle; the heart pumps the blood.

options.content: Its valves stop blood flowing backwards.
options.rationale: Capillaries have no valves.

options.content: Its wide lumen lets blood flow quickly through the tissues.
options.rationale: The lumen is very narrow and the flow slow, which helps exchange.

options.content: Its wall is one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance.
options.rationale: This allows rapid exchange of substances.

explanation: Capillary walls are one cell thick, so oxygen, glucose and wastes diffuse a very short distance. Their narrow lumen and slow flow give time for exchange, and their huge networks give a large surface area.
hints: What is the main job of capillaries?

stem: Complete the sentences about blood vessels.

payload.template: Arteries carry blood {{blank:dir}} the heart. Veins contain {{blank:valves}} to stop blood flowing backwards. Capillaries have walls that are {{blank:thick}} thick.

explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins have valves to prevent backflow; capillary walls are one cell thick for exchange.
hints: Remember: Arteries go Away.

stem: Blood flows through a capillary at 0.3 mm per second. The capillary is 0.9 mm long. Calculate how long it takes blood to pass through it.
explanation: Time $= \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}} = \dfrac{0.9}{0.3} = 3$ s. This slow flow gives time for substances to be exchanged with the tissues.
hints: Time = distance ÷ speed.

stem: A blood vessel has a wall 0.4 mm thick, a lumen 8 mm wide and pocket-shaped flaps on its inner wall. What type of vessel is it?

options.rationale: A wide lumen, a thin wall and valves (the flaps) are features of a vein.
An artery has a thick wall, a narrow lumen and no valves along its length.
A capillary is far narrower, with a wall one cell thick.
An arteriole is a small artery with a muscular wall and no valves.

explanation: The thin wall compared with the wide lumen, and the valves (pocket-shaped flaps), identify a vein.
hints: What are the pocket-shaped flaps?

stem: How is tissue fluid formed at the arterial end of a capillary?

options.content: Cells in the tissue actively pump water and small solutes into the capillary blood.
options.rationale: At the arterial end, fluid moves out of the capillary, not in.

options.content: Red blood cells burst and release their contents.
options.rationale: Red blood cells stay inside the capillary.

options.content: High blood pressure forces water and small solutes out through the capillary wall.
options.rationale: This is pressure filtration.

options.content: Lymph vessels release fluid into the spaces between the tissue cells.
options.rationale: Lymph vessels drain fluid away from the tissues.

explanation: At the arterial end of a capillary the blood pressure is high. It forces water, glucose, amino acids, oxygen and mineral ions out through the thin capillary wall (pressure filtration), forming tissue fluid that bathes the cells.
hints: The pressure is highest at the arterial end.

stem: Which of these is normally absent from tissue fluid?

options.rationale: Tissue fluid is mostly water.
They are too large to pass through the capillary wall.
Glucose molecules are small enough to be filtered out.
Oxygen passes into the tissue fluid and on to the cells.

explanation: Pressure filtration forces small molecules and ions out of the capillary, but red blood cells, platelets and large plasma proteins are too large to pass through the wall, so they stay in the blood.
hints: Which item is far too large to pass through the capillary wall?

stem: True or false: oxygen moves from the tissue fluid into body cells by diffusion.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. Cells use oxygen in respiration, so its concentration inside them is lower than in the tissue fluid.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. Oxygen diffuses down its concentration gradient from the tissue fluid into the respiring cells.

explanation: Respiring cells use up oxygen, so its concentration in the cells is lower than in the tissue fluid. Oxygen therefore diffuses into the cells, while carbon dioxide diffuses out.
hints: Cells use oxygen up. Which way is the concentration gradient?

stem:
A student measured three blood vessels, X, Y and Z, in a prepared slide.

| Vessel | Wall thickness / mm | Lumen diameter / mm | Valves |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| X | 1.2 | 3.0 | absent |
| Y | 0.6 | 6.0 | present |
| Z | 0.0005 | 0.008 | absent |

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the ratio of lumen diameter to wall thickness for vessel Y.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: (Supplement) Explain how the wall of vessel X suits the blood pressure inside it.

points.description: Thick (muscular) wall withstands the high pressure of blood from the heart
Elastic tissue stretches and recoils with each surge, maintaining pressure / smoothing the flow

parts.explanation: X is an artery. Its thick wall withstands the high pressure of blood pumped from the heart, and its elastic tissue stretches with each surge and recoils, keeping the pressure up and the flow smooth.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: (Supplement) Explain how vessel Z is adapted for exchanging substances with the tissues.

points.description: Wall one cell thick (0.0005 mm) gives a short diffusion distance
Narrow lumen (0.008 mm) means red cells pass close to the wall / slow flow gives time for exchange / many capillaries give a large surface area

parts.explanation: Z is a capillary. Its wall is only one cell thick, so substances diffuse a very short distance, and its narrow lumen makes red blood cells pass slowly and close to the wall, giving time for exchange.

explanation: X (thick wall, narrow lumen, no valves) is an artery; Y (thin wall, wide lumen, valves) is a vein; Z (wall 0.0005 mm, lumen 0.008 mm) is a capillary. For Y, $\dfrac{6.0}{0.6} = 10$.
hints: Use all three clues: wall, lumen and valves.
For (b), divide the lumen diameter by the wall thickness.

stem: Body cells are bathed in tissue fluid, which forms from the blood in capillaries.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe how tissue fluid is formed.

points.description: At the arterial end of the capillary the blood pressure is high
Water and small molecules / ions (glucose, amino acids, oxygen) are forced out through the capillary wall: pressure filtration

parts.explanation: At the arterial end of a capillary, the high blood pressure forces water and small dissolved substances such as glucose, amino acids, oxygen and mineral ions out through the thin capillary wall. This is pressure filtration.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why tissue fluid contains no red blood cells.

points.description: Red blood cells are too large to pass through the capillary wall

parts.explanation: Red blood cells are too large to pass through the capillary wall, so they stay in the blood.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Describe how glucose and carbon dioxide are exchanged between the tissue fluid and a respiring cell.

points.description: Glucose diffuses from the tissue fluid into the cell (higher to lower concentration)
Carbon dioxide diffuses out of the cell into the tissue fluid (made by respiration, so more concentrated in the cell)

parts.explanation: The cell uses glucose in respiration, so glucose diffuses from the tissue fluid into the cell. Respiration produces carbon dioxide, so it is more concentrated in the cell and diffuses out into the tissue fluid.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: State what happens to tissue fluid that does not return to the capillaries.

points.description: It drains into lymph vessels (as lymph) and is returned to the blood (near the heart)

parts.explanation: It drains into lymph vessels as lymph, which is returned to the blood in veins near the heart.

explanation: Pressure filtration at the arterial end forms tissue fluid without cells or large proteins. Cells exchange substances with it by diffusion; most fluid returns to the capillaries at the venous end and the rest drains into lymph vessels.
hints: Think of pressure at the arterial end and diffusion at the cells.

stem: (Supplement) Explain how the structures of arteries, veins and capillaries are related to the pressure of the blood they carry and to their functions. [6]

points.description: Arteries have thick (muscular) walls to withstand high pressure
Arteries have elastic tissue that stretches and recoils, maintaining pressure / smoothing flow
Veins carry blood at low pressure, so their walls are thinner
Veins have a wide lumen giving little resistance to flow
Veins have valves to prevent backflow of low-pressure blood
Capillary walls are one cell thick for a short diffusion distance (possible because the pressure is lower)
Capillaries are narrow / form large networks, giving slow flow and a large surface area for exchange

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Arteries receive blood from the ventricles at high pressure, in surges. Their thick, muscular walls withstand this pressure, and their elastic tissue stretches with each surge and recoils, which maintains the pressure and smooths the flow. Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure, so their walls can be thinner; their wide lumen offers little resistance, and valves stop the low-pressure blood flowing backwards. Capillaries exchange materials with the tissues. Their walls are only one cell thick, which is possible because the pressure has fallen, giving a short diffusion distance. They are narrow, so blood flows slowly past the cells, and they form huge networks with a large surface area.

explanation: Each vessel's wall, lumen and valves match the pressure of its blood: high in arteries, low in veins, and falling in the capillaries, where exchange happens.
hints: Give two features for each vessel and link each to pressure or function.

stem: (Supplement) Blood in the veins of the legs is at low pressure, yet it returns to the heart against gravity. What mainly helps it to do this?

options.content: The thick elastic walls of the veins recoil after each heartbeat and push the blood upwards.
options.rationale: Veins have thin walls with little elastic tissue.

options.content: Capillaries in the legs pump the blood up.
options.rationale: Capillaries have no muscle and cannot pump.

options.content: Contracting leg muscles squeeze the veins, and valves stop the blood flowing back down.
options.rationale: Blood can only be pushed towards the heart.

options.content: The semilunar valves pull blood up from the legs.
options.rationale: The semilunar valves are in the heart and cannot pull blood.

explanation: When the leg muscles contract they squeeze the veins between them. The valves in the veins only open towards the heart, so the blood is pushed upwards and cannot fall back.
hints: What happens to a vein when the muscles around it contract?

stem: Which blood vessel carries blood **to** the lungs?

options.rationale: It carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
The pulmonary vein carries blood from the lungs to the heart.
The aorta carries blood to the rest of the body.
The vena cava brings blood from the body to the heart.

explanation: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Arteries carry blood away from the heart.
hints: Blood going to the lungs is leaving the heart.

stem: (Supplement) Shop assistants and security guards who stand still for many hours each day are more likely than other people to develop swollen veins in their legs, in which the valves no longer close properly. Explain how blood normally returns to the heart from the legs, and suggest why standing still for long periods can lead to this problem. [5]

points.description: Blood in leg veins is at low pressure and must flow upwards against gravity
Contraction of the leg muscles squeezes the veins, pushing blood towards the heart
Valves close to stop blood flowing back down
When standing still, the leg muscles contract little, so blood is not pushed up
Blood collects / pools in the leg veins, increasing pressure on the vein walls and valves
The veins stretch so the valves cannot close, and the vein swells

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Blood in the veins of the legs is at low pressure and must travel upwards against gravity. When the leg muscles contract, they squeeze the veins and push blood towards the heart, and the valves close behind it so that it cannot flow back down. When a person stands still for hours, the leg muscles hardly contract, so blood is not pushed upwards and collects in the leg veins. The pressure of this pooled blood stretches the vein walls until the valves can no longer close properly, so the veins become swollen.

explanation: Normal return depends on muscle contraction squeezing the veins and valves preventing backflow. Standing still removes the squeezing, so blood pools, stretching the veins and their valves.
hints: What normally pushes blood up the leg veins?
What happens to blood if that push is missing for hours?

stem:
(Supplement) The table shows the mean blood pressure in different parts of the systemic circulation.

| Vessel | Aorta | Large arteries | Arterioles | Capillaries | Venules | Veins | Vena cava |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mean pressure / kPa | 13.3 | 12.0 | 6.0 | 3.3 | 1.6 | 1.0 | 0.4 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage fall in mean pressure between the aorta and the capillaries. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Between which two neighbouring parts of the circulation does the pressure fall the most?

options.rationale: The fall here is only 1.3 kPa.
The fall here is 1.7 kPa.
The fall here is only 0.6 kPa.
The pressure falls by 6.0 kPa as blood enters the narrow arterioles.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Use the data to explain why veins have valves but arteries do not.

points.description: Pressure in veins is very low (about 1.0 kPa), so blood could flow backwards
Valves stop backflow; in arteries the high pressure (12–13 kPa) keeps blood moving forwards

parts.explanation: The pressure in veins is very low, about 1.0 kPa, so the blood could flow backwards, especially in the legs; valves prevent this. In arteries the pressure is high, 12 to 13 kPa, so blood is driven forwards without valves.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain how the low pressure in the capillaries allows them to carry out their function.

points.description: Capillary walls can be only one cell thick without bursting
giving a short diffusion distance for exchange (and slow flow, which gives time for exchange)

parts.explanation: Because the pressure has fallen to about 3.3 kPa, capillary walls can be only one cell thick without bursting. This gives a short diffusion distance, and the slow flow gives time for substances to be exchanged with the tissues.

explanation: Fall from aorta to capillaries $= 13.3 - 3.3 = 10.0$ kPa, which is $\dfrac{10.0}{13.3} \times 100 = 75.2\%$. The biggest single drop is from the large arteries to the arterioles (6.0 kPa). Low pressure in veins makes valves necessary; low pressure in capillaries allows walls one cell thick for exchange.
hints: Work out the fall between each pair of neighbouring vessels.
Link low pressure to the structure of the vessel.
